title: wsutil: Add a macOS backend to the process lookup
description:
Adds the macOS backend of `wsutil/process_lookup.h` (!26493), which so far is implemented for Windows and Linux. It is one new file behind the existing backend interface; nothing uses it on macOS until `dumpcap --process-info` (!26518) is merged.

**How the sockets are found.** There is no table of all the sockets with their processes that can be read through a public interface: the `net.inet.{tcp,udp}.pcblist_n` sysctls that netstat reads have private structures that are not in the SDK. So this does what lsof does, with libproc (`<libproc.h>`, `<sys/proc_info.h>`, part of libSystem, no new dependency): `proc_listallpids()`, then for each process `proc_pidinfo(PROC_PIDLISTFDS)` and for each socket descriptor `proc_pidfdinfo(PROC_PIDFDSOCKETINFO)`. As it goes through the descriptors of each process, a socket that several processes hold is reported for each of them, which is what the API wants.

**Privileges.** That works for the caller's own processes and, as root, for everybody's, the same as the Linux backend without and with CAP_SYS_PTRACE. On a Mac where dumpcap runs as the user (ChmodBPF), the user's own programs are identified; system daemons such as mDNSResponder are identified when it runs as root. Sockets that belong to the kernel (e.g. the SMB client's) have no process either way.

**What describes a process.** Parent, user, start time and name come from the `kern.proc.pid` sysctl and `proc_name()`, the path from `proc_pidpath()`; those work for every process. The command line comes from `kern.procargs2`, which works for the processes whose sockets can be seen.

**Cost.** A refresh takes about 2 ms, as a user or as root, on an M4 with 680 processes, and refreshes are rate-limited by the common code.

**Tests.** The existing `test_wsutil` process lookup tests (IPv4, IPv6, wildcard UDP, a socket shared with a forked child) now run on macOS and pass, as a user and as root. This adds one for all platforms: an IPv4 connection accepted by an IPv6 socket that is not IPV6_V6ONLY, which must be found by its IPv4 addresses. Linux reports such a socket with IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses, and macOS with IPv4 addresses and a flag, so it is the case a backend is most likely to get wrong; it passes on Linux, Windows and macOS.

Also tested by hand on macOS 26 together with !26518: its three capture tests pass, and a capture on en0 attributes a curl transfer from its SYN onwards (and, as root, mDNSResponder). Processes that live for less than the capture's read timeout are missed, as documented in !26518. Its man pages say "Not supported on other platforms"; whichever of the two is merged second will need that sentence updated, and I'll do that.

macOS is not built in fork pipelines, so this was built with the macOS job's options (`-DENABLE_WERROR=ON`, Apple clang) on an Apple Silicon Mac.

commits_data.message:
wsutil: Add a macOS backend to the process lookup

Find the processes that have a TCP or UDP socket open on macOS the way
lsof does, with libproc: list the file descriptors of each process with
proc_pidinfo() and ask for the socket behind each one with
proc_pidfdinfo(). There is no table of all the sockets with their
processes that has a public interface; the structures of the pcblist_n
sysctls that netstat reads are private.

That covers the caller's own processes and, as root, everybody's, like
the Linux backend without and with CAP_SYS_PTRACE. A refresh takes about
2 ms on a desktop with several hundred processes.

The parent, user, start time, name and path of a process come from the
kern.proc.pid sysctl, proc_name() and proc_pidpath(), which work for
every process, and the command line from kern.procargs2, which works
for the ones whose sockets can be seen.

Add a test with an IPv4 connection accepted by an IPv6 socket, for all
platforms: systems report its addresses in different ways (as
IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses on Linux, as IPv4 addresses with a flag on
macOS), and it has to be found by its IPv4 addresses.
